name: Maya Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Maya. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union or party, and what you tell me stays confidential. Your name won't go on anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Westfield Family Clinic, on a big new housing estate at the edge of the city. The clinic's run by a company that has six of them, and our patients are mostly young families, so it's fevers, rashes, baby checks, pregnant mums and parents who are exhausted. I see about thirty-two people a day, and I use an AI assistant for nearly all my notes and letters.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the pace and I like the families; a toddler who comes in floppy at five o'clock and leaves bouncing is the best feeling in the job. What wears me out is the company's targets, appointments per hour and how thin they can spread us over the estate. Some days I feel like a shelf-stacker with a stethoscope.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And at home, how are things?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Jonah, who's a pharmacist at a supermarket pharmacy. We rent a new-build flat on the same estate and we've got about five months of costs saved. On Tuesday evenings I do online consultations for a telehealth company, which pays for our holidays. My dad's a joiner, and he's always said working for yourself beats working for a company, so I've been sketching out a small private clinic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start. The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that's a bit of a letdown. I use these tools every day and they're already better than this sounds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful and the hype was overblown, both at once. At work I'd keep showing the other doctors my shortcuts, because the company's targets don't go away just because AI stalls. Online I'd post the odd tip for other GPs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means the company keeps squeezing us the old-fashioned way. If AI stalls, I'm still a shelf-stacker with a stethoscope, just with slightly better notes. Which pushes me harder towards running my own clinic, frankly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on at Westfield, keep the Tuesday telehealth shifts, and keep saving. I'd want about 15,000 put by before I opened anything of my own, so I'd aim to get there in two years. And I'd keep using the AI assistant, because even ten minutes a day matters against those targets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about my own job, but restless, like waiting for a bus that's been cancelled. And Jonah's hours sit on my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you tell first that the private clinic is still the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad. He set up his joinery workshop at twenty-nine with a van and a loan from his brother. He'd say there's no point waiting for the world to change before you make your own move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any money pressures right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rent on the flat went up when the estate got popular, and Jonah's hours got cut a bit when the supermarket brought in a dispensing machine. We're fine, but it's tighter than it was last year.

say: The tools are **useful** and the hype was **overblown**, both at once.
I'd keep sharing **shortcuts** with colleagues and post the odd tip online.
think: The company keeps **squeezing us** the old-fashioned way.
That pushes me harder towards opening **my own clinic**.
do: Keep her Westfield job and the **Tuesday telehealth** shifts.
Save towards **15,000** to open her own clinic within two years.
feel: **Restless**, like waiting for a bus that's been cancelled.
**Jonah's cut hours** sit on her mind.
S0.quote: If AI stalls, I'm still a shelf-stacker with a stethoscope, just with slightly better notes.
fieldNote: Her frustration is with **company targets**, not with AI.

Her **dad's joinery workshop** is the model for her ambition.

steps.text: Keep working full-time at Westfield Family Clinic
Keep her Tuesday evening telehealth shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'd bet on, actually. And it's the one I'd like most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the best thing to happen to general practice in years, if doctors get to use the time for patients instead of more targets. I'd say it at work, online, everywhere. I'd also say people who lose admin jobs should get apprenticeships, not just a payment and a pat on the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's my chance. If AI does the booking, the letters and the checking, a small clinic needs one doctor, one nurse and a laptop. I could open my own place with longer appointments, and families would pay for that, because they're sick of seven-minute ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd rent a room above the pharmacy on the estate on Saturdays and run a private family clinic with thirty-minute appointments. I'd put about 6,000 of savings into equipment and insurance, and set up AI for booking, notes and billing so I don't need a receptionist. I'd keep my Westfield job during the week until the clinic pays for itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. A bit nervous about the money, but mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Six thousand is a big part of your savings. What does Jonah think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's more careful than me, so he'd want a deadline: if it's not covering its costs in a year, I stop. That's fair. He also likes the idea that one of us isn't at the mercy of a big company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said admin staff should get apprenticeships. Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two receptionists at Westfield, Gemma and Sue, who basically run the place. The company would cut them the minute the AI could take the calls. I'd rather see them trained as healthcare assistants than handed a leaflet about benefits.

say: It's the **best thing** for general practice in years, if the time goes to patients.
People who lose admin jobs deserve **apprenticeships**, not just a payment.
think: With AI, a small clinic needs **one doctor**, one nurse and a laptop.
Families would pay for **longer appointments** at my own place.
do: Rent a **room above the pharmacy** on Saturdays for a private family clinic.
Put about **6,000** of savings into equipment and insurance.
Set up **AI booking**, notes and billing instead of hiring a receptionist.
feel: **Excited**, with a little **nerves** about the money.
S1.quote: If AI does the booking, the letters and the checking, a small clinic needs one doctor, one nurse and a laptop.
fieldNote: She sees Steady Disruption as **her opening** to work for herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's a lot faster than I'd planned for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say doctors must stay accountable and the companies selling AI must be liable when it goes wrong, same as any business. And I'd say the government should pay for retraining, not just hand out cheques. I'd probably be quite vocal about it online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my private clinic idea dies. Families won't pay me for thirty minutes of thinking when they can talk to an AI for free at midnight. What's left is hands: examining a baby, stitching a cut, and even that only until the robots come in 2031. And Jonah's job goes too, probably sooner than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the clinic plan, keep the savings, and push them up to six months of costs. I'd ask Westfield to move me onto the home-visits team for frail elderly patients, because that's the most hands-on work the company has. And Jonah and I would give up the flat and move in with my parents for a year to save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan, which is how I cope. The bit that hurts is that I'd been about to build something of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI every day. Doesn't that give you an edge here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For about a year, maybe. Being good at using the tool matters when the tool needs a driver. Once it doesn't, I'm just a doctor with good habits and a nice set of shortcuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving in with your parents. How would that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would be thrilled and my mum would rearrange my old room within the hour. Jonah would be polite about it for a month and then start fixing their boiler. Family is what you lean on when things go sideways; that's how I was brought up.

say: AI companies must be **liable** when things go wrong, like any business.
Government should **pay for retraining**, not just hand out cheques.
think: My **private clinic** idea dies if AI thinks better by 2028.
**Jonah's job** probably goes even sooner than mine.
do: Drop the clinic plan and build savings to **six months** of costs.
Ask to join Westfield's **home-visits team** for frail elderly patients.
Move in with **her parents** for a year to save.
feel: **Hurt** that she was about to build something of her own.
S2.quote: Families won't pay me for thirty minutes of thinking when they can talk to an AI for free at midnight.
fieldNote: Being an **early adopter** buys her only about a year, she thinks.
Both incomes are exposed, and she expects **Jonah's job** to go first.
Her safety net is **family**, not the state, though she wants paid retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That I can do something with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same about accountability and retraining, but I'd add that small businesses should be allowed to use these tools as freely as the big companies. Otherwise the six-clinic companies swallow everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to open my clinic, earn from it for three or four years and get my savings back before 2031. After that, the clinic's value is whatever's hands-on: baby checks, cuts, injections, scans. I'd build my clinic around hands from day one, because by 2031 the thinking part of medicine won't be worth paying for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd take a course in point-of-care ultrasound, which means scanning at the bedside, for about 2,500. Next year I'd open the Saturday clinic above the pharmacy, run on AI for all the admin, with scanning as the thing families come for. And I'd set myself a rule: if it isn't paying by 2029, I sell the equipment and go back to salaried work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good, sharp way. I like a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say about the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say what he said when he bought his second van: make your money while the work's there, and don't fall in love with the van. He's changed trades twice himself, from building sites to kitchens to fitted wardrobes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Jonah, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's already looking at retraining as a clinical pharmacist in a hospital, where it's more ward rounds and talking to patients than counting pills. Five years gives him time to do that. We'd both be moving towards the bits that need a person in the room.

think: Five years lets me **earn back** a clinic's costs before 2031.
I'd build the clinic around **hands-on care** from day one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a full business cycle and then some.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for anyone willing to work for it, and that people should start learning now rather than wait for a scheme. I'd say it to the youth group at church too, because they're picking their courses now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be calm. Ten years is long enough to open my clinic, grow it, maybe open a second one, and sell before 2036 if I need to. I'm 27, so even after it lands I'd be young enough to start something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd open the Saturday clinic as planned, with 6,000 of savings, and go full-time on it within three years if it works. I'd use AI for every bit of admin. And I'd start saving for a house with Jonah again, because ten years is long enough for that to make sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years is a gift if you use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the teenagers in your youth group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the teenagers at church to learn a skill they can do with their hands, and how to run a business. Nobody is going to hand them a career in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you change course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the big clinic companies got the health board to block small practices from using the best AI. Then I'd be competing with one hand tied, and I'd probably sell early and go into teaching doctors instead.

People should **start learning now** rather than wait for a scheme.

At 27, I'd be **young enough** to start again after it lands.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years would kill the clinic before it opened, hit Jonah's job and mine at once, and send us back to my parents' spare room. What would help is the government paying for real retraining, like apprenticeships for doctors and pharmacists in hands-on work, and rules that let small practices use the same AI as the big companies.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who pays. If AI makes a consultation nearly free, someone has to decide who pays for the human parts. I'd rather it was families choosing than a big company deciding for them.
